newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi's Buyoya to open talks with rebels soon.
newsitem.headline: Burundi's Buyoya to open talks with rebels soon.

text.p: Burundi's military leader Pierre Buyoya told an Independence Day rally on Tuesday he would soon enter direct talks with armed groups in an attempt to end the country's bitter civil war.

"We will start negotiations openly with armed groups and all political parties, but we will never forget the reservations of some Burundians about these negotiations," Buyoya told a crowd of around 20,000 mainly-ethnic Tutsis at a stadium in the capital celebrating 35-years of independence from Belgium.
He gave no date for the start of talks.
Buyoya said he would boost the military's size and technical strength and appealed for support from regional neighbours to stop conflict in the tiny country.

The wife of Burundi's National Assembly speaker Leonce Ngendakumana was wounded and her bodyguard killed late on Monday when their vehicle hit an anti-tank mine in the capital, local journalists reported.
The mine exploded three days after eight soldiers and four civilians were killed in a mine blast in Gihanga commune in Bubanza province.

Buyoya has been under intense pressure since announcing in May that his government had signed a pre-ceasefire agreement with the main Hutu rebel group the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD), one foreign analyst said.

Fellow ethnic Tutsis denounce negotiations with CNDD whom they accuse of genocide against Tutsis, while the moderate opposition Frodebu party resents being sidelined by direct talks with rebels, the analyst said.
Uprona chairman Charles Mukasi said he boycotted the celebration because the government tried to muzzle him for his opposition to negotiations.
"Buyoya has already negotiated with the armed groups and signed an agreement. What he doesn't say is that he wants to implement the agreement," Mukasi said.
Senior Frodebu officials including ousted president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya also said they boycotted the event, arguing ethnic Hutus were effectively barred from state functions.

Regional states imposed sanctions on Burundi last July after an army coup brought Buyoya to power, but relaxed them in April. They demanded evidence of direct talks with rebels before the embargo was lifted.
More than 150,000 people have died in Burundi since October 1993 when the country's first freely-elected Hutu president was murdered by Tutsi troops in an attempted coup.
